utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone, including you, Mr. Indjic. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution ready to resume the cross-examination of Mr. Indjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You then may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know where Mr. Ierace is going to continue, but apart from the pages, can my learned colleague give me also the dates of the interventions that he quoted yesterday at the end of the hearing. It would be much easier for us like this to orient ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can't give the dates, but I can give the page references. They are the references to the pages of the transcript, Microsoft Word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the pages. We got them yesterday. I will do some research, random research. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday, I put to you some evidence that we have heard from Lieutenant-General Mole. I will repeat to you some aspects of his evidence. He said that General Galic -- he was a person that he met with, and that you were quite often present at those meetings. And at those meetings, General Galic would tell him quite specifically that Sarajevo would be shelled if demands made on behalf of the Serb side were not met. He gave evidence that this type of threat was made by General Galic five to ten times. He also gave evidence that that threat was made both individually by the accused as well as by Serb liaison officers. And he said that you attended his meetings with General Galic more often than not, although your attendance dropped off and became more infrequent towards the end of Lieutenant-General Mole's period in Sarajevo, which I remind you was between September 1992 and the end of December 1992. What do you say to that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several claims have been now made. I have to deal with them one by one in order to give you my explanation and my opinion. First of all, I should like to repeat what I stated yesterday, that the name Mole is quite familiar to me, but I cannot remember who the person is. Similarly, I cannot remember whether I attended the meetings that Mr. Mole had with General Galic. I do not deny the possibility, however, I do not specifically recall it. Second, it has been put that General Galic said that he would shell Sarajevo if demands made on behalf of the Serb side were not met. Not at a single meeting that I attended with General Galic did I hear such a claim being made by General Galic. Third, it has also been put to me that individual Serb liaison officers said the same, expressed the same threat. I claim here with full responsibility that such a claim was never made by myself. As for the last statement that I -- that my attendance dropped off eventually, I cannot comment because I really do not remember how often I attended these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to check something, but I don't see this in the pages that I have. Could Mr. Ierace give us the exact pages and the transcript where he got this information from. Thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thought I had done that yesterday, and I should add one further page reference for the frequency of attendance of the witness at those meetings, which is 10.955. I may have given that. And also 10.98, I think it is, 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, did you find the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I started with the beginning. Yesterday, I noted the pages 9857, 9518. I cannot on the basis of this continue, but Mr. Ierace can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday, you gave some evidence about daily meetings which occurred at a command -- at the command level at the Lukavica headquarters. You said that there were two types, the first was when there was intensive activity going on, and the second was what you call normal meetings when there was not such activity, and those normal meetings were attended by someone from your liaison group. Did you attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Colonel Zarkovic was absent, that is, in the period when I carried out the duty of the chief of the group, I attended those meetings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You also said that there was another type of meeting, an analysis meeting, which was held perhaps biannually. Did you attend those meetings in Colonel Zarkovic's absence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the analysis in response to the question whether brigade commanders attend the meetings, and I said that according to what I know, they were present when annual or biannual analyses were done. However, these meetings were not attended by anyone from the liaison group with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In your office at Lukavica headquarters, did you have a television set?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During a period of time, yes, and then at other times, no. At the very beginning, I think we did have, it but I don't know when we got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm really sorry, but in order for us to understand, I should like -- I would like Mr. Ierace to quote page 1955, because I really cannot -- 10.985. The number that Mr. Ierace gave us is 10.955. 10.955. And in these pages, I'm afraid I didn't find that. Could Mr. Ierace be perhaps more precise and give us the paragraph in question, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what date?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I opened several of them, but I think we should focus on the 7th of March -- excuse me, the 7th of July -- no, the 3rd of July, Mr. President. It's the 109th day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is it exactly that you couldn't find?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sorry, I'm trying to find the relevant day. I didn't give you the right references, but I just found it. 10.955. And on that page, I didn't find the references concerning the question that has just been asked by Mr. Ierace, with respect of the testimony of Lieutenant-Colonel Mole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would now like to know exactly what part of the question do you contest to be correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to the presence of the witness concerning the claims of Mr. Mole regarding the illegitimate shelling of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I'm just wondering. Was part of your question that when that happened, those specific meetings that the witness was present, or that these things were said during meetings in which most of them the witness was present? It's not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I respond to that in the absence of the witness, and in private session. I respectfully submit that perhaps we should establish some ground rules, because there is much of this testimony to be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Indjic, may I ask you to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the reference is actually the 2nd of February, 2002, the 108th day. I didn't find this on the relevant page in relation to the question by Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I have some difficulties to accept that the 2nd of February, 2002, was the 108th day of this Court hearing. Numbers stand for something. The 108th day was approximately a couple of months after we started. Mr. Ierace --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my apologies. The 2nd of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, firstly in response to your specific question, I put to the witness yesterday that Mr. Mole had regular meetings with the accused and Captain Indjic was present at those meetings quite often. And indeed, that was further the subject of evidence by Mr. Mole that Captain Indjic was present more often than not at the first meetings and then they dropped off. The end result of that evidence is that this witness may or may not have been present when these things were said. And that was clearly -- that was made clear to this witness. Further, that the type of threat was made by the accused five to ten times, in other words, it would seem that at quite a large number of those meetings. That's the basis upon which it's put to the witness. And I think the witness's answer Indjicates that he understood that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I ask you first, you said that you need a specific quote, and the general rule here is that if there are good reasons to assume that the testimony of a witness is misrepresented, that you can ask for a quote if there's any serious contest to what has been said. Could you please Indjicate what part of the question you contest to be a fair reflection, I'm not saying literal word, but a fair reflection of what the testimony was?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not contest generally speaking that there should have been such declarations. But what I would like to do is to be able to exercise my rights properly, to know exactly where these details come from. If the Prosecution is not able to give us the relevant references or are only giving us wrong references I don't see how we can proceed. The same principle applied to the Defence and I think it should apply to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it's different. That principle did not apply to the Defence. Whenever there's a serious question of whether the way the earlier evidence is presented could be not correct, then the other party is allowed to ask for a specific source. Since you demonstrated that you want for every single summary of an earlier testimony of a witness, you want the source, you have read them, I take it. You were guided by me yesterday that you prepare for reading all the testimony that refers to the present witness. You now asked for a reference of something that was not truly contested as being a fair reflection of what the witness has said. And of course, you can check whether the quotations are right. If you need assistance, it has been given to you. Page references have been given to you yesterday. So there's no way that you cannot check that. But you cannot for every single question ask without serious grounds to give the page reference. But I'm certain that wherever Mr. Ierace is in a position to use those words that would enable you to search or to tell you on what days what witnesses have testified so you can better search, that everyone will certainly assist you. And if needed, I will do so as well. So if you have difficulties in finding the dates on which certain witnesses testified, I will be glad to help you. The Prosecution is allowed to use its time in a proper way. That's my ruling --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what I say is the page 10.955 is the information that I got. But there's nothing in it. That's very simple. I cannot verify all of the transcripts of a particular year because I don't know what questions there will be by the Prosecution. When I asked the reference, I get the wrong one, and there is nothing in it. And once again, I'm sorry, I can't look at it, the screen has been blocked. The computer has been blocked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will check that and we will see how we can assist you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, on page 10.955. Is your LiveNote available? It's broken down. Then we'll ask the technicians to assist Mr. Piletta-Zanin restoring his LiveNote. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, are we still in private session, if so, there's one further matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have not been in private session. That is a mistake. Then we should redact --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps there's no need to redact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No need to redact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't think so. But perhaps we could go into private session to raise one further matter to minimise interruptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: [Open session].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as page 10.955 is concerned, I do understand that this is the testimony of Witness Y. And Witness Y, that might have caused the confusion, was the witness in respect of whom questions were put about a document of which we had no copies available for the parties yesterday about crossing the airport. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. To the extent that we can now see the reference is not a realistic one, I think that as far as this intervention is concerned, or these interventions are concerned, my learned colleague should give me the exact reference. It's not only his duty; it's his obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not in general terms his obligation. Whenever there's a serious reason to believe that the way one of the parties puts something to the witness which not properly reflects what is the testimony, then we'll verify the source. So you may Indjicate, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, why you think that it's not fair, something you did not do in respect of what Mr. Ierace has put to the witness until now. And we will then check it. Let's try -- it's in the interest of the Defence as well, I take it, that there will be time remaining for re-examination if needed. And we have to use our time. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I said that as far as these ten or more interventions are concerned, they are the problem. I need to know the references Mr. Ierace should tell me where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I told you what the ruling is. You now repeat that you want a page for every single word Mr. Ierace speaks. He is not obliged to give at any every single reference the page. And if you have difficulties, I will, where there's a really good reason to check it at the spot, you, having read and having properly prepared this examination, so knowing what the testimony is of whatever other witness about this witness, that's the basis on which we'll continue. And if necessary, we'll check it. You may write it down. During the break, we'll check whether it's correct or not. And if not, be certain that the Prosecution will be reprimanded for that and could have to face consequences why not properly reflecting the evidence of other witnesses. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I wish to know if you have the number of the page that that testimony of General Mole's is in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That the affirmation that the witness was there more often or not or the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The five to ten times.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, the five to ten times. Excuse me, Your Honour. That was that the type of threat was made by the accused five to ten times, not that the witness was present. 9837.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Now you have the page, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, did you have any responsibilities to the accused or the Sarajevo Romanija Corps generally to inform them of what was in the media as to the conflict? In other words, what was being reported in the media?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Following the media and all the means of information was the duty of the deputy commander for morale and legal issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was that officer's name in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Kosovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he remain in that position through to August 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when he retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did anyone else occupy that position between September 1992 and August 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was he based at the Lukavica headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was his office on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was it on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he also have a television in his room, in his office?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There were satellite dishes on the roof of the headquarters, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suggest to you that between September 1992 and August 1994, at some stage, there were satellite dishes on the roof. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only during the period when the military observers were in Lukavica, and they installed their own system for monitoring, their own satellite television monitoring system.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When did they make that installation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did Colonel Kosavac speak English?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Surely you would know that, sir, you being in the same headquarters, you not knowing, as I understand it, of others who spoke English in the headquarters? Would you not know if he did?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't something that I should have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he ever ask you to come into his office to view a programme on the television, on a television, in the English language?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you think it was important for the leadership of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to be aware of what was being reported in the media as to events in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never even thought about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suggest to you that you're being untruthful in that answer. I suggest to you that surely that would have occurred to you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what would have occurred to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That it would have been useful to follow what was being reported in the media as to events in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably would have been useful. It's useful to follow everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And that's something you realised at the time, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you have dealings with journalists yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as the liaison officer, in order to enable them to contact those who were responsible for giving them press cards, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. What American television journalists did you have contact with in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. There were several persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember any names?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Christiane Amanpour, for example, Jacky Shumansky, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And were there journalists from other states as well? Television journalists?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you understand that they were moving on the territory controlled by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: With film crews?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was in the teams, but I know that there were journalists in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you telling us that you don't know whether they were moving around with film crews, taking pictures for television, these television journalists?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, damn it, if they are journalists, it is normal that they are going to shoot this, they are going to film things, but I can't make such a claim because I wasn't with them when they were filming.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It was an important consideration, was it not, for security purposes to know whether people who were being approved to move on your territory were filming?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand now. You're confused with regard to my role. I wasn't a security officer. I was a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. And indeed Ms. Amanpour interviewed General Galic, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As the liaison officer of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, you tell us you don't know whether General Galic was interviewed by Christiane Amanpour, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Even though you were responsible for giving her accreditation to be there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't give foreign journalist accreditations. Accreditations were issued by the press centre in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, you understood that these people were also filming on the other side of the confrontation lines, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have assumed that they were filming there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you make that assumption?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, you tell us that it never occurred to you that it would be important to be aware of what these people were filming, what they were doing on the other side of the confrontation line, what they were reporting. I suggest to you that that's something you clearly would have been aware of, the importance of monitoring the media, whether it was your job or not.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it is serious to make claims as to what I thought or did not think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you watch the television that was in your office for a period of time, in particular, news reports?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, when I had the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, did you understand that someone in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was monitoring the media in order to determine if there were allegations being aired in the media that Bosnian Serb armed forces were responsible for deliberately or indiscriminately targeting civilians in the city of Sarajevo on the other side of the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware of any investigations that were carried out within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps as a result of such media reports?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any investigations that were carried out on the basis of reports from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If there were such investigations, would you expect to have known about them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So apart from protests made by the United Nations, do you say that you had no involvement with investigations that may have been carried out as a result of media reports?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were asked whether there was a protest lodged by the United Nations as to a shelling of a number of civilians said to have occurred on the 4th of February, 1994, in Dobrinja. And you said -- well, perhaps you could say again, was there such a protest in relation to that incident?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw such a protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you doubt that there was such a protest from a UN agency made to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do doubt that there was such a protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When did you first become aware of that shelling?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be a little more precise and tell me the shelling you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well -- excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to ask you for 30 seconds. I think that General Galic would like to confer with Ms. Pilipovic. And in order to make sure that there is not very much noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Meanwhile, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd like to tell the Chamber that there is nothing on page 9837. I've just verified that. There's nothing in that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you using the French or the English transcript, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you know that we don't have access --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Written, perhaps. You checked it on your computer, so it should be the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, so as not to waste any time, Mr. Ierace can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're ready, Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He has asked you for details of the 4th of February shelling in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I ask the witness be shown a document, Prosecution Exhibit P3778.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is this a recall exhibit, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: This is a fresh exhibit. For the assistance of the Trial Chamber and the Defence, this is a photocopy taken from the commission of experts report for the 4th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the extent that this document has just been produced, is there a translation into the Serbian language for General Galic because it is in English, and if not, we will be at a slight disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the parts you referred to, if you could read them, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, so that they can be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, you said Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Did you mean me, to read them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, do you have before you a document which in the left-hand column at number 723 bears the date 4.2.94 [Friday]? Do you see that on the front page?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right, I will take you through some parts of that document. Do you see under (b), "targets hit: A food line in Dobrinja"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: "Description of damage: Significant loss of civilian lives."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: "Sources, Agence France Presse, Reuters."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And then under (d) "casualties: Nine people including two children were killed and 18 others were wounded when shells hit a line of people waiting for flour to be distributed in Dobrinja at 11.00 a.m. Sources: Agence France Presse, Reuters."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And then going over the page, second paragraph: "According to UNPROFOR, the flour line shell was fired from a Serb-held area." And then a quote: "A crater analysis by UN military monitors has shown that the mortars came from the Serb side about 2.5 miles to the southeast in the Lukavica." UN military spokesman, Major Jose Labandiera said. He also said: "The line was hit by three 120 millimetre mortar shells." Labandiera added that "UNPROFOR BiH commander Sir Michael Rose had inspected the blood splattered site right after the early afternoon attack and a crater analysis quickly followed. Bosnian Serbs denied responsibility for the shelling. In a statement carried by the Tanjug news agency, the Bosnian Serb army command stated that `no mortars were fired from Serb army positions in the sector around 11.00 a.m.', the time of the attack. Nikola Koljevic, vice-president of the Republic 'vigorously' protested, at what he called a `setup job' that had cost civilian lives. He said that UNPROFOR `can check for themselves, but Serb forces don't have artillery pieces at Vranjes' from which the BiH army alleged the mortars were fired." Now, does that refresh your memory as to the incident that you were asked by Mr. Piletta-Zanin yesterday and that I have been asking about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you now recollect a protest being made by the UN in relation to that shelling?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you accept that a protest would have been made, although you don't remember it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. The question is highly hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, to ask someone whether he accepts something happened when he just said that he has no recollection, is that of any use? Would that assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would have thought that it would assist the Chamber. But if you think not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- Perhaps I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, if a protest was made, given the evidence -- your evidence yesterday as to how protests came through you, it would have passed your desk, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group for cooperation with UNPROFOR would have received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you mean the group at Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am referring to the group in Lukavica, the one that I was part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. And the head of that group at that stage was you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether that was the period when Colonel Zarkovic had already returned from the ministry or whether I had that position at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When communications were directed by the Bosnian Serb liaison officers at the PTT building in Sarajevo to the Lukavica headquarters, they came to you, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were received by the group for cooperating with UNPROFOR. Whether that was myself or someone else at the time, that is less relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Even if Colonel Zarkovic was with the SRK at that stage, you were the next most senior officer in that group, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recall telling us yesterday that the liaison officers at the PTT were not professional liaison officers? Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You were a professional liaison officer, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I and my colleague Luledzija, who was -- who is six years my senior. We hold the same rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, I'm suggesting to you that if a protest was made, and I suggest to you further a protest was made, you knew about it. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about the protests that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And knew nothing of protests that you didn't directly receive. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us yesterday that there were a number of protests made about sniping. You went on to explain that there was an understanding on the part of those who made the protests, that snipers included -- or sniping included the use of regular infantry weapons. To your knowledge, did the Sarajevo Romanija Corps have snipers, that is, persons trained in the art of sniping in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer this question by providing two parts to the answer: I didn't give such a statement such as it has been portrayed in the first part. I said that when there were protests, any infantry fire was treated as sniper fire. As far as the second part of the question is concerned, I don't know whether Sarajevo Romanija Corps had any men who had been trained in sniper action, but I do know that it did not have any snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How many times in that relevant period, September 1992 to August 1994, did you receive protests alleging that snipers had shot civilians? Just an approximate number.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're trying to make me say again that a sniper hit civilians. I don't remember any protests according to which snipers hit civilians. But protests to the effect that sniper fire had been opened, I may have received about 100 such protests.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And in the responses that you conveyed back from the duty officer, from General Galic, was there -- was it ever said that the SRK did not have snipers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the answers to those protests, after the matter had been checked, it was determined that this concerned fighting and the exchange of infantry fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question. Please listen to it carefully. In the responses that you conveyed back from the duty officer or General Galic, was it ever said that the SRK did not have snipers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary to make such a statement because in the protests, it was never -- they never asked whether we had snipers or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, do I take that as a no, that it was not ever said?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to take you to some further evidence that we have heard. Yesterday, you were asked if you recalled an UNMO by the name of Henneberry, that is, Major Patrick Henneberry, and you told us that you didn't. Does it refresh your memory if I tell you that at one point, he was the commander of UNMOs on the Lima side? That is, the commander of UNMOs based in Lukavica headquarters opposite your office. Do you remember him now?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military observers in Lukavica rotated every four or six months. So if you look at that period of time and the number of them who served there, you will understand. It would be very difficult for me to remember him. If you had a photograph, it would of course be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. You're saying that you still don't remember him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And I think you said yesterday that you didn't socialise -- well, you don't remember socialising with such a person?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could please be more precise. What exactly do you mean when you say "socialising"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll remind you of your evidence yesterday. You were asked this question: "Was this one of your close friends with whom you may have gone and taken -- had meals together or had drinks, or you shared some emotions together, something like that? Yes or no." Answer: "Certainly not. Otherwise I would have remembered who this was." Is that still your evidence, that you don't remember then certainly he wasn't someone that you would have socialised with, had meals together or drinks, or shared some emotions together?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, and I abide by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps that document could be returned. And I ask the witness be shown a photograph which will be P3449A. Might that be placed on the ELMO. Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Firstly, do you recognise yourself in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And are you the person towards the middle of the photograph with your hands around the shoulders of two other people, with the moustache?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now please disregard the date that appears in the bottom right-hand corner of the photograph. That date is incorrect. Now, do you recognise anyone else who appears in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to move from right to left? We see Colonel Marcetic, the chief of staff of the SRK. Next to him is Tatjana, I believe was her name. She worked at the SRK press centre. Next to her is an UNPROFOR member, judging from the insignia on his shoulders. Then myself. Next to me, Zoran Kos. And next to Zoran, Vesna Matovic who also worked in the press centre, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Who was Zoran Kos?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Kos was a noncommissioned officer who worked with -- at the security service. He's deceased. He's no longer alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And did he die during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He became severely disabled during the war, but I think he died after the war. I don't know the cause of death, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the room in which you are seen in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that this was a room which was used by UN military observers in Lukavica. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does it look as if some people have had a meal?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't look like a lunch, but I think it could have been somebody's birthday or some other type of anniversary. So I think that we just had a snack.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think I can see some steak on the table. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can see is some salami and bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. It looks as if some people have been drinking. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see a couple of glasses on the table, a bottle containing I don't know what. A can of beer maybe. I don't know whether this is a bottle of wine or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It looks as if the people here have had a meal. They're having a drink, they're sitting back after the meal and Zoran is smoking, having an after dinner cigarette. That's what the picture suggests, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at that part, if you look at Zoran, yes. However, if you take a look at Colonel Marcetic, you will see that he looks a bit worried. At least to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. And you have no idea of the name of the person around whose shoulders you have your arms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in light of the story we heard so far, I assume this is Mr. Henneberry, otherwise you wouldn't have showed me the photograph. However, without a previous story and without your mentioning his name, I don't think that I would be able to tell you who the person is. I wouldn't be able to tell you his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does he look familiar, even if you don't recognise him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does look familiar. I can recognise him on this picture. But if you had shown me any other photograph, I wouldn't have been able to link the name with the face. I am familiar with the name and the face, but I couldn't make that connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What if I tell you he was Canadian. Does that help?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see that judging by his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Indjic, Major Henneberry has given evidence. And I'd like your response to some aspects of his evidence. He has told us that he was the senior military observer and later commander of Lima UNMOs between the 30th of July 1992, that's when he was a military observer, and by December 1992, he was based permanently at Lukavica barracks where he stayed until mid-February 1993. Does that assist in your recollection? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He has told us that before he moved permanently to Lukavica barracks, he would visit the barracks sometimes once a week, sometimes several times a week, and he would speak to you. Tell me, did you ever visit the Lima observation posts in the relevant period, September 1992 to August 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not precise enough because there was a Lima HQ and seven additional observation posts that belonged to the Lima. Which Lima position did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't ask you about the headquarters. Did you visit - I'll rephrase it - any of the Lima observation --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there were seven such positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Indjic, is did you visit any of the seven observation posts? Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I visited most of the Lima positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Major Henneberry tells us that at Lima 7, he observed numerous times soldiers firing weapons, indirect weapons, artillery and so on, without aiming, sometimes whilst intoxicated, and in some cases he would see the Bosnian Serb soldiers at Lima 7 actually just kick the weapons, and where they stopped was fine, and they would fire that way. Did you ever see any of that behaviour at Lima 7?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the sake of precision, could you please remind me -- actually, I'm afraid I don't quite understand your question. There was an addition of some sort at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, did you ever visit Lima 7?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to give you my answer. But in order to be precise, I cannot remember all of the markings where each of the Lima posts were. Could you tell me the geographical location of Lima 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Lima 7 is roughly to the east of Sarajevo. It's north of the Miljacka River. So in that sense, in the northeast. Does that assist you with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blagovac perhaps? Do you remember the name of Blagovac?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, to save time, I have a copy of P742, if we cannot obtain the tendered one quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it may be put on the ELMO, and the Defence will have an opportunity to see the -- to compare the -- the original is available already, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. I'm grateful to Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you see on the map in front of you L7?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Accept from me we've heard evidence that that was the position Lima 7. Did you ever go there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you shocked to hear this account of how weapons were sometimes fired from Lima 7?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about being shocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you surprised?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are now being hypothetical. You're asking me whether I'm surprised if that was the case. Well, if that was the case, indeed, then I am surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Major Henneberry gave evidence that the soldiers on Lima 7, and indeed other positions, other Lima observation posts, told him frequently that they would just fire because they wanted to at no particular target on occasion. And sometimes they would fire in other observation posts just by the time of day in the general area of target. He said that Limas 10 and 11, that is the Bosnian Serb forces at those two observation posts, would open fire frequently around suppertime. Do you recollect ever having heard allegations of that nature made to you in respect -- or allegations of that nature in respect of Lima 7, Lima 10, Lima 11, or any of the Bosnian Serb forces at Lima observation posts?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He gave evidence that the commanders of the Bosnian Serb forces at Limas 3 and 7 admitted that their soldiers were firing indiscriminately. He said many times -- I'm sorry, I withdraw that. Start again. Major Henneberry gave evidence that many times he was standing at the gun position while the guns were being fired, and the forces with smiles on their faces, that is, the gun crews, would say to him "we're not firing." Have you heard that said before in relation to the gun crews at any of the Lima posts?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Major Henneberry gave evidence that before he moved in to Lukavica, when he would visit Lukavica once, perhaps several times a week, he would complain to you occasionally as to Bosnian Serb forces being responsible for the deaths of civilians. Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only is my answer no, but I also have to add that no one ever complained to me that Bosnian Serb forces had been responsible for any civilian death in that form.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. He also told us that after he moved in to Lukavica, he complained to you about the shelling of civilian areas in Sarajevo "dozens and dozens, if not hundreds, of times." What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He gave evidence that some days, he would spend six hours with you, some days he would meet with you 20 or 30 times. Do you still not recognise the person in the photograph around whose shoulders you had your left arm?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true that I don't remember. I told you that I do remember the face on the photograph when I saw it, and I had already told you that I remembered the name also. But I couldn't make the connection between the name and the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that answer later. In the meantime, Major Henneberry said that your response was: "Much rhetoric about why the Serbs were shelling the Muslim civilians and military, how the Serbs had been persecuted over the centuries." Did you ever respond to complaints made by UN officers that civilian areas were being shelled by giving the complainer a history lesson from the Bosnian Serb perspective? Did you ever do that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that I spoke about the history of the Serb people, but I never linked their history with the answer concerning possible combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you that you linked it not only with possible combat operations, but with allegations that civilians were deliberately or indiscriminately targeted. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He said that in the first period, that he raised these complaints with you, that he made these protests, you would sometimes deny it was happening or suggest that the observers were mistaken in what they saw, or that it was the fault of an uncontrollable element. Let me take those separately. By way of response to protests that civilians were being deliberately or indiscriminately targeted, did you ever sometimes deny it was happening?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received any protest about deliberate or indiscriminate targeting of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you received it in those words. I'm suggesting to you that on numerous occasions, Major Henneberry complained to your face --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, may I ask you not to seek eye contact with the other party when you are examined by Mr. Ierace. It was not the first time. This happened before several times. Would you refrain from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that the complaint was in those words, but I think you understand me that complaints were made to you that civilians were being deliberately or indiscriminately targeted. Sometimes you would deny that was happening. You did that, didn't you, sometimes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever complained to me about any deliberate or indiscriminate targeting of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. To be clear, so we understand your evidence, you're saying, are you, between September 1992 and August 1994, no one ever complained to you about any deliberate or indiscriminate targeting of civilians? Is that correct? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And your office was on the opposite side of the corridor to the UNMOs' headquarters. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And you were on duty or available as they were 24 hours a day. Is that correct? When you were in the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The liaison group for UNPROFOR was available around the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Major Henneberry said that he got to know you quite well, that in fact the two of you developed a rapport. Did that happen between you and Major Henneberry?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not doubt that Mr. Henneberry could have stated something to that effect. However, I remind you that I stated yesterday that I had met over 1.000 UN officers. I don't know what kind of rapport we had because I simply cannot remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So Mr. Indjic, you're telling us that maybe you did, maybe you had a rapport with Major Henneberry, but if you did, you don't remember it. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Mr. Henneberry was the commander of the Lukavica HQ Lima post, then I'm sure we had regular contacts. However, I claim here that I didn't establish any profound rapport, any more significant relationship with anyone over there including Major Henneberry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until 11.00, but before doing so, I inform Mr. Piletta-Zanin that when he has difficulties in finding the sources, he should be aware that there is a slight difference in paging between the LiveNote that you find on your desk and the sources Mr. Ierace gave. Yes, I just tried to understand the gesture you just made, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could assist as well, if my learned colleague is using LiveNote, there are many different spellings of the witness's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. You can find for Indjic I-N-D-I-C or I-N-D-J-I-C. There are several ways of spelling. If you use both of them, there's a better opportunity to find it. For example, page 9837 on the written version is 9833 in the LiveNote version. And if you have had, although I didn't hear you, if you have had any problem in finding the source on which Mr. Ierace seemed to rely during his last questions, it's 8574 in the LiveNote version. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before the witness is brought in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- Might I clarify how much time I have remaining. If I was permitted to go for as long as I require, that would probably be some hours. But I think I've probably have less than two hours left, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we certainly have. We want to finish by today. The Defence claimed four hours, took more than four hours. I think until now the Defence took approximately four and a half hours. But I have to check that precisely. I think until now, yesterday it was -- let me just see. We have 1 hour and 37 approximately. And 1 hour 17 today. That would make two hours and 50 approximately, so the remaining time approximately one hour and a half, one and three quarters of an hour approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And Mr. President, will I be required to stay within that time according to the normal rules with this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see how it develops, Mr. Ierace. But let's keep in mind -- if it would be of any guidance, whether a table leaves an impression that some people have been eating there, even if the witness would deny that, that would not make a great difference I would say. And if sometimes we hear questions that the Chamber thinks of that perhaps were not strictly necessary, so you would please keep that in mind. And then we'll see where we come. We would have after the next break, we would have a little bit over one hour. We'll then -- yes, that's -- we would like you to stay within these time limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, also might I take advantage of this break to point out that we still have not received the updated witness list for next week, and now it is, of course, Friday. And I think that should have been delivered on Monday, last Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why is it not delivered, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, the Prosecution was provided with a letter with the schedule for witnesses for next week. I don't have the letter here at the moment. I'm surprised to hear my colleague put this question now. I'll try and find it, and I'll try and inform you of it at the next break so as not to waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's not waste time at this very moment. And there seems to be a problem anyhow with the arrival of witnesses and the Victims and Witnesses Unit would like to speak about that. But we should not deal with that at this moment in Court. But I'm just made aware of --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just discussed this matter, and I think we agreed on everything during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether there's an agreement on everything. But we'll find out that later. The witness may be brought in to the courtroom. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, Major Henneberry gave evidence that your explanations changed, that is, your explanations in response to his protests as to the deliberate killing of civilians. His evidence was that after you developed a rapport with him, you admitted to Major Henneberry that you knew civilians were being shelled and were dying, and that you believed it was wrong, but it simply was going to continue. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement in the last two lines is not a statement that I ever made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: See, I'm suggesting to you that you became unusually friendly with Major Henneberry, and you became indiscreet, you became very candid with him. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was candid in relation to all members of the UNPROFOR. There was no reason for me to behave in another way. But what is certain is that I never became friends with Major Henneberry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We have heard evidence that you told Major Henneberry that the ultimate goal was to either destroy the city or rid it of Muslims. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's completely false.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You Indjicated to Major Henneberry that in spite of your awareness of the wrongdoings of the SRK, you intended to stay, and you were looking forward to senior appointments and promotion within the corps. Were you looking forward, as of January and February 1993, to senior appointments and promotion within the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you think that you were an ambitious officer in early 1993 in terms of your own career?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very beginning of my career, I was an ambitious officer in realistic terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At one stage, were you the private secretary to the minister of defence of RS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was General Milovanovic ever the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I can remember. In the -- during the relevant period, but during the post-war period, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And when he was minister of defence, did you work for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President, we're speaking about the post-war period. This is not just after the relevant period, but this is after all the events that we might be interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that Mr. Ierace seeks to establish a fact directly contained in the Indjictment, but he is pursuing other purposes with this line of questioning. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace. The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When he was minister of Defence, did you work for him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While General Milovanovic was minister of defence, I was a member of the intelligence department of the Republika Srpska army, so I didn't have any form of direct contact with General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When did he cease to be the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the previous allocations came to an end, when Mr. Bilic was assigned as minister of defence. I can't remember when the elections were held exactly. I cannot remember the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, you tell us you cannot remember the year in which he ceased to be the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the year when the elections were held and when Mr. Bilic was assigned as minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the last elections in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the elections before the -- the penultimate elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I no longer see what the relevance is. I don't see where we are heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't intend to ask any more questions on that issue, for the moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, then, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Major Henneberry has given evidence that you told him words to the effect that your attitude was that the killing -- the deliberate killing of civilians was the corps [Realtime transcript read in error "core"] plan, it was a necessary evil. Was it part of a corps plan that civilians be deliberately targeted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any kind of corps plan. And as a result, I don't know about a part of a corps plan either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise, but we have a translation problem. I don't know if Mr. Ierace used the "core" or "corps". I think it should be clear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I -- we have heard some potential problems with the word core which could be written corps and core. Could the B/C/S booth just tell me how they understood the last question -- the last answer about a "core plan." What was the witness referring to what I know by now to be the corps more or less or to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, you don't, Mr. President. I have changed the channel. And the B/C/S booth understood it as a corps plan, C-O-R-P-S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have some difficulties in finding the answer from the B/C/S booth. Yes. Yes. Yes. And that's how you translated it? Yes. I do understand, Mr. Ierace, that you asked for a corps plan. That's how it was said. It was not right in the transcript. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you were the only one who would have known about how it was translated to the witness. I think everyone understood it in a similar way. A tiny little yellow note would have done. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I've --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 18739 to 18752.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was listening to the French and English channels, and I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could have got the attention in both languages. A yellow note doesn't prevent you from asking the attention both in English and in French. There's no misunderstanding in whatever way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, did you...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that everyone was understanding and responding as to the corps as far as I understand. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, did you sometimes have a drink, an alcoholic drink, with UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's customary for us to offer guests a drink, so I certainly did have a few drinks with military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever drink to excess with UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever become drunk with UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not with UNMOs or with anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You've told us indeed that you were on duty or on call 24 hours a day. Did you ever become drunk whilst in the headquarters at Lukavica in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never been drunk, neither in the Lukavica command or in the course of my private life.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the admissions, the statements, which according to Major Henneberry were made by you to the effect that it was wrong to target civilians, but it happened, it was part of a corps plan, words to that effect, were made by you sometimes when you had been drinking and sometimes when you were not drinking. Do you understand what I'm putting to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting that the words attributed to you by Major Henneberry, according to him, were uttered by you on a number of occasions, sometimes when you were drinking alcohol with him and sometimes when you were not. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, but as I have already said, I never said anything of the kind to Major Henneberry regardless of whether there was drinking or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might we move into private session. I think this would be for about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, you told us you received training in intelligence before the war, and you've told us that you worked in intelligence at some point after the war. Did you work as an intelligence officer during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you in Belgrade at any point in 1992? From January 1992 until December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was that at the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And indeed, were you stationed within the JNA in Belgrade at the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you stationed in Belgrade in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There must have been a misunderstanding. I was in Belgrade on private business, and my duty and the positions were where I held is something that I discussed on the first day. I was on duty in Rajlovac and Sarajevo, that is, I spent the entire time of my tour of duty in Sarajevo except when I was on training. I was never on duty in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. The cover of a liaison officer with UN -- I withdraw that. The position of liaison officer with the UN in its various forms, both military and in terms of humanitarian aid, would have been convenient for an intelligence officer seeking to obtain information and general intelligence as to what the UN knew. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you, whether it was true or not, that your job was an ideal cover for an intelligence officer in the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there are many more covers that are actually better.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your job involved contact with dozens if not hundreds of UN officers, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That alone made it an ideal cover, didn't it? You didn't need an excuse to talk to people.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the purposes of understanding, the mission of the UN was completely open, and they did not have any secrets which would have required intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember Commandant John Hamill, UNMO at Lima 5, and then team leader at Lima 8, in Sarajevo between May and August 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a problem in interpretation. I'm now following the B/C/S interpretation, and I heard Lima -- they said Lima 10, which is not correct. In the transcript, we read Lima 8. So I think it has been translated as Lima 10 instead of Lima 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question was about Lima 8, Mr. Ierace. Mr. Indjic, please understand, the question that's referring to Lima 5 and then team leader of Lima 8. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was an Irish officer, though I don't think I could recognise him if I saw him in the street now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: After those positions at Lima 5 and Lima 8, he worked in the Lukavica headquarters or Lukavica barracks as it was sometimes known. Do you remember him from working in the room opposite you at the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't rule out that possibility. However, I cannot claim with any certainty that that was the case. As far as I'm concerned, he was just one of the observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We've heard evidence that Commandant Hamill would discuss with the liaison officer cease-fires or request cessation of shelling, and he would do that after he was informed from UNMO headquarters inside the city that a particular area was being sniped and shelled. He would do that with the liaison office by walking to the liaison office which was directly across the hallway from his office. Do you recollect such conversations with Commandant Hamill, conversations on those topics between May and August 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a customary way of forwarding protests. I cannot claim with certainty that it was a conversation with Mr. Hamill. But for the purposes of better understanding, let us be clear about the period. From May 1993 until August 1993 was a very difficult period for myself privately. My mother was dying. When I came back from Belgrade, I saw her. I met her. I waited for her because she had come from abroad. And she died soon. And I buried her sometime in late July.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Indeed Commandant Hamill has told us that if he could not speak to you, in those circumstances he would speak to Captain Luledzija. And I think you've told us that there was another liaison officer of that name who spoke English. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We've heard that when he complained to the liaison officer, the liaison officer would ring the brigade in question and would request them to cease firing. Did you ever do that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we did not have any competence in terms of command with respect of the brigades. By calling a brigade, we were able to obtain information as to whether there was any combat activity in the area of responsibility of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Did you call a brigade sometimes to find out if there was any combat activity in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally never did that, because I did not want to interfere with the command and control system.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
