utterances.text: Indeed, if you had done that, it would be quite contrary to the procedure that you told us yesterday, wouldn't it, the regular procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have constituted an interference with the control and command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that's what you did do, just that.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suggest that you're being a little modest about the power that you had, that your power went beyond what you have described to us, and that power included the power to contact brigades directly rather than go through the duty operations officer. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just your opinion, and it is erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Commandant Hamill has given evidence that the liaison officer would sometimes make the call to the brigade in front of him. He would actually ring the brigade in front of him, or request the person on the switchboard to ring the brigade and speak to somebody in the brigade. Was that you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This just confirms the inaccuracy of the testimony by Mr. Hamill because there was no possibility from our office to contact any kind of switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So if you rang the brigade from your office, you would ring direct from your phone. Is that the position, if you did that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I did that, then it would be directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was there a switchboard somewhere in the headquarters in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you contact that switchboard from your phone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I see. If the UNMOs wanted, could they contact the switchboard from their office?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Commandant Hamill said, as I've mentioned earlier, if you were there, they would speak to you; if not, it would be Captain Luledzija. And if they received information, that is, the UNMOs received information that shelling was going on in a particular area, perhaps an area monitored by one of the Papa observation posts, they would go to your office and say "there is shelling going on in that area. What's happening? It must be stopped. And at that stage, they would often know already that it was happening naturally, because they were the corps headquarters, or if they didn't know it was because they had -- perhaps you might say it was an independent activity going on. Generally they were aware of what was going on, and had a prepared answer, if you will, if they didn't wish to stop the shelling or shooting. Or sometimes they did anyway, they stopped it or caused it to be stopped." Do you agree as to that explanation of responses by you or your fellow liaison officer in that office to protests? That sometimes in particular you would have prepared answers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The testimony of Mr. Hamill is an approximation and not a professional -- not a reflection of a professional attitude. As to the questions of military observers, one would have to be a wizard to be prepare answers in advance. Of course, if there was combat activity, we would use our communication services and we would have the information on this combat activity before we would receive it from the military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, one scenario in which you might have advance warning in let's say a shelling of the city, of course, is if Lukavica headquarters was either aware in advance or had ordered it and armed you with an appropriate response to the inevitable protest. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't because the SRK carried out defensive operations and returned fire only when it had been fired upon. And one could never know when the other side would open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. According to your explanation of how it all worked, what Commandant Hamill described could not have happened. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can tell me specifically what you are referring to, you said a number of things that were said by Mr. Hamill.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I'm referring specifically to the suggestion that you would have prepared answers, that is, the officers in the liaison office opposite the UNMO office, they were aware of what was going on and had a prepared answer if they didn't wish to stop the shelling or shooting. That's what I'm specifically referring to. On your account of how it worked, that description could not have happened. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, no, something like that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember Commandant Jacques Kolp, K-O-L-P, UNPROFOR liaison officer between March 1993 and November 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're now talking about a Belgian officer, if my memory serves me right, although I'm not sure if I would be able to recognise him if I were to see him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We've heard evidence that he would meet with you practically every day, and the main issue that he discussed with you was clearance for various convoys. Does that assist you with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all likelihood, that was the case because all permissions for convoy movement, that is, all such requests, came -- excuse me, all permissions reached the liaison group for UNPROFOR before the office at Pale was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you remind us what month that was, when they were no longer referred to Lukavica and were referred to Pale, what month and what year?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was somewhere in the beginning of 1993. As for Lukavica, they sent their requests to Pale. However, the clearances arrived in Lukavica because it was at the level of the corps command that it was necessary to order the local checkpoints, what to do, and to inform them of the fact that the convoy had been permitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, again to assist you with your recollection, he was Belgian. He formed a view that you were a direct associate of the commander of the Serbian army corps, as he described it, General Mladic. Can you think of anything which would have given him that impression?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he probably found it impressive to think about people at the top. I don't know what sort of things go on in the mind of a person who makes such crazy assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He said that his initial contact with the liaison office was in the PTT building, but he could never obtain an answer from that office because those Bosnian Serb liaison officers would say they had to contact you in Lukavica. Would you expect that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, he couldn't receive an answer in Lukavica either until that answer was received from the main staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But you see, his evidence wasn't that they told him they had to contact Colonel Zarkovic, but you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have already agreed that Colonel Zarkovic at the beginning of 1993 was appointed as minister of defence. That's natural, because I didn't deny that I performed the duties of chief during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you said it was from mid-1993, not the beginning of 1993. When was it that Colonel Zarkovic left the headquarters and went to the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the first half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suggest to you it was May. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can neither confirm nor deny that. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In any event, Major Kolp, Commandant Kolp made clear that he received these replies from the office in the PTT very early in his period and he started in March 1993 and as a result of those responses, he stopped going to them and instead would travel to Lukavica. Sir, if Colonel Zarkovic was still in the position of your boss at the time that Commandant Kolp was being told by the PTT office that they had to speak to you, do you accept that that suggests that in their minds, the liaison officers in the PTT, you were the person, not Colonel Zarkovic, that they felt they had to obtain decisions from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't accept that. Perhaps they told him to contact me as they knew that Colonel Zarkovic didn't speak English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Commandant Kolp -- I'm sorry. Just in relation to that answer, Commandant Kolp's evidence wasn't that they told him to contact you, but rather they had to contact you in order to obtain an answer to give him. It had nothing to do with the speaking of English.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer the question as to what Major Kolp and the liaison officer in the PTT spoke about if I didn't attend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, he said, the evidence was, that having made the decision to go straight to Lukavica rather than waste time at the PTT, he would have contact with you. Indeed, as I've Indjicated earlier, he would meet you practically every day. And in your office, he would see all kinds of people with problems, UNMOs, members of international organisations. Firstly, is that possible? I think you would agree that UNMOs would be in your office. What about members of international organisations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said, it's correct to say that I had contact with over a thousand members of the United Nations, and that includes UNPROFOR and the military observers and the UNHCR and the international committee of the Red Cross, and various volunteer organisations such as Caritas, nongovernmental organisations, and et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And did that include organisations providing medical assistance to Serb civilians, Bosnian Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember an agency called the Emergency Medical Response Agency, represented by John Ashton?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember an agency that was -- had that name. I had a visit card, and I knew that its headquarters were in Berlin. I don't think it really existed. There was a story according to which John Ashton was a CIA member.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. In the meantime, Commandant Kolp said he also saw Serbian paramilitaries in your office. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you say who in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, I can't give you any names. But his evidence was that Serbian paramilitaries dressed partially in civilian clothes, wore military trousers and coats, and black caps with human skulls on them. Does that assist you in identifying who he might be speaking about? Also, they had long hair and beards.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these characteristics of these people is proof in your opinion that this concerns a paramilitary unit, I don't agree with that. The Chetnik detachment on Grbavica was a legal unit, and it was part of the SRK, or rather of the 1st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, I take it that the description that I've just provided you fits members of that unit. Is that correct? The Chetnik detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't a paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I see. He said that -- excuse me. He said that he saw them in your office on three or four occasions between April, May 1993 and early 1994. Does that fit timewise?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's correct. He should have seen them far more frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And he said he saw some of the same people on more than one occasion, and people similarly dressed in the Hadzici area on the Sarajevo/Pale Road. Given what you've told us about the Chetnik detachment at Grbavica, would you agree with me it would be unsurprising if he saw some of those same people on the Sarajevo/Pale Road?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why that should be surprising. It wouldn't be surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I agree with you. Now, why were they in your office, you, the liaison officer, with the UN?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tons of civilians came and members of the military came to my office, and they took advantage of the opportunity to telephone members of their family who were in the Muslim territory because the only telephone line in the area of Serbian Sarajevo which was connected to the part of town which was under Muslim control, the only phone that could be used to establish such contact was in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did your phone go through the switch? You've told us that you could contact the switch. Did it go through the switch?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I couldn't contact the switchboard, and this phone didn't go through the switch. It went through the Sarajevo airport to the PTT building, and it was part of the regular civilian telephone network.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I apologise for that. I stand corrected if I misrepresented to you your earlier evidence. So, are you saying that your office was used by various people to contact relatives in Sarajevo, including soldiers from the front line? Would that be a fair comment on your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Therefore, you, for that reason alone, had contact with soldiers from the front line. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did not those individuals move freely around the Lukavica headquarters unescorted, carrying their weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people were members of the Republika Srpska army, and I don't see why they shouldn't move freely through the Lukavica command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to this question because the witness replied by mentioning and including civilians and members of the military, and as the question has been put by Mr. Ierace, it creates confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question has been answered. From the answer, it does not appear that it created great confusion. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Commandant Kolp gave evidence that police on checkpoints would have to repeat -- would have to report to you from time to time in terms of convoys, and he named as one such individual Colonel Zdravko Zgonjanin. Would you expect -- I'll withdraw that. Would that be the case, perhaps in the relation to the passage of convoys, that they would contact you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, because the checkpoints would receive authorisation through the corps command. And a copy of what had been authorised and what hadn't was located in the group for cooperating with UNPROFOR. And if a convoy appeared for which authorisation had not already been provided, we would then check to see whether there was an authorisation for this convoy or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Commandant Kolp has also said that he lodged complaints, protests, about incidents occurring in Nedzarici and the Grbavica areas, as well as from the Jewish cemetery. Firstly, do you remember any such protests? And that's, I should say, in relation to the targeting of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many times I've already repeated this. I never received a protest in which targeting civilians was explicitly mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with regard to the previous question, in fact, the two previous questions, and as far as the convoy issue is concerned, Mr. Ierace withdrew something, he rephrased his question, but I don't see what the word is that he wanted to Indjicate in the transcript. This is important for the re-examination that we might conduct. We have in the transcript the sign which Indjicates the absence of something, and then "of convoys."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find exactly -- that's page 63, line 12 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems it's page 63, line 11 and 12. My transcript is not quite working.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It was something to the effect of in the case of convoys. And I appreciate my learned colleague is asking from the point of view of re-examination, not the understanding of the witness. The witness clearly understood the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then having explained this, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now Commandant Kolp --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sorry, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the Jewish cemetery, are you aware of General Rose visiting the Jewish cemetery on one occasion to inspect it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can remember that. I remember it in particular because I don't think he wanted to wear a flak jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Approximately when was that? Was it around March 1994 perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can remember is that there was no snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And did you understand that the reason that he took the trouble to do that was because it was a notorious area in terms of protests about sniping of civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's absolutely false. That was an area where the demarcation line was the narrowest. The positions were only separated by a few metres, the positions of the warring factions. General Rose visited those lines in order to display, to show, that certain steps had been taken to obtain a truce in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, Commandant Kolp gave evidence that once when he was in your office, you issued an order regarding shooting. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's rubbish. It's a lie. And I couldn't have issued such an order, and I never did issue such an order. And I'm not aware of the fact that Major Kolp speaks the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, we heard evidence that it was interpreted to him through his interpreter. So you understand that more than one UNMO has given evidence that you had direct contact with the armed forces, with the troops. You continue to deny that you did, in terms of protests, responding to protests.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm claiming that I didn't have any contact with subordinate units in accordance with the command and control system. And that I was not in a position to issue subordinate units orders of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, the witness seems to be very consistent in where he denies allegations made by you. I don't know whether it's really necessary if you are under time restraint to seek such answers to be repeated three, four, five, six or even more times. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that being the case, if you don't require me to do it, then I won't continue to take the witness through the other evidence of various witnesses which touches on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can ask it -- I think the witness in respect of at least now a few, Mr. Hamill, Mr. Henneberry, Mr. Kolp, consistently told us that he never gave -- never had direct contacts with brigades, that he never gave orders, what he explained what his position was. I do not expect that the witness would answer in a different way if you would confront him with similar information given by other Prosecution witnesses. So therefore, I take it, but if it's not true, Mr. Indjic, please tell us. I take it that all the questions asked to you about your functions, about your -- the powers you had, the way your group received protests or did not receive certain protests as far as you know, if you would be asked about the other witnesses giving similar information, although not always exactly the same, that that would not change any of your answers given until now. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All my answers would have to do with my personal competence, responsibility, and that of other groups for liaising -- the other members of the group for liaising with UNPROFOR. All the answers that I would provide with respect to this matter would be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that being the case, then - and I'm referring to the first part of what you just said - I will refrain from confronting the witness in the way in which I have been doing, confronting the witness with the evidence which supports the Prosecution case that has been given in respect of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least in respect of those issues that have been dealt with by the other testimonies. Of course, if you would have anything else in mind... But until now, your questions mainly concentrated on how protests were received, through whom, about the content of these protests, about what action was taken in respect of that. I mean, that whole series of questions I think we went through it now, of course in slightly -- with a slight variety as to the exact content of the testimony you have confronted the witness with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I don't think it's of great use to repeat it for other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recall the chief of staff of UNPROFOR, General Van Baal? He occupied that position from February to September 1994.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember General Van Baal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And do you recall him conveying protests to you, protests concerning the sniping of civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, just to make sure, the witness has testified now, I think, five or six times that he never, ever received any protests on deliberate sniping or deliberate targeting of civilians. So this would, in my view, be one of the questions that might not have been necessary. And the witness confirms again that also from General Van Baal, he did not receive such protests.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next question I'm about to put to the witness comes out of the one I just put. And I would be grateful for your guidance whether you wish to hear questions such as the one I'm about to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you respond to General Van Baal we don't have the snipers under our control? Given your earlier answer, did you ever say those words to General Van Baal, "we don't have the snipers under our control"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't have answered in such a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned earlier in response to the name John Ashton that you had some information involving the CIA. What was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, John Ashton is a CIA agent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal impression, my opinion on the basis of my personal experience in intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When did you first form that opinion?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the second or third time that I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What month and what year was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the month. I think it was in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The summer of 1992, you've told us that you weren't working in intelligence during the relevant period. Did you communicate this opinion to the intelligence section of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take it you told General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Galic never had any contact with John Ashton, as far as I know. Neither was this requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Did you receive any instructions from anyone on how to handle John Ashton, that is, given your opinion that he worked or was involved with the CIA?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take it that you took all possible steps to ensure that he did not travel on SRK territory, given your view. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he wasn't the only intelligence officer in the Sarajevo area, and it would be absurd to forbid someone to move around for the simple reason that that person was in intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you mean by that that although you formed the view that he was employed by the CIA, you also formed the view that he was not adverse to the interests of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we weren't at war with America. And for that reason, CIA intelligence officer isn't the enemy of Bosnian Serbs. He wasn't an intelligence officer of the AID.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What specifically was it that led you to the opinion that he was a CIA intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His performance, his way of working in the field, he had far more authority -- more authority than he was prepared to admit as a photographer, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Indjic, can you please be more specific. Going through those aspects one at a time, what do you mean by his performance?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He appeared in the Sarajevo area, and his cover story was that he a freelance photographer. And I think that as a freelance photographer, he had visited all the battlefields throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think there were many freelance photographers, were there not, who came to Sarajevo from a background of working in other conflicts? Why did you single him out differently from those?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, I said that this was my opinion, and this was the impression that I had, I thought he was a CIA agent. But I don't have any documents about this. I'm talking about my personal opinion and the impression I had with regard to John Ashton.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The next factor you mentioned was his way of working in the field. Can you offer any specific explanation in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His approach, the way he dealt with people, his interest in specific issues. All these factors contributed to my general opinion of him, but I would like to repeat that this is my personal opinion about John Ashton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, it's 25 minutes to 1.00. You're almost through your time. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00. And then I'd like you to conclude within 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace. Once the witness has been brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, would you allow me a minute, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, we've heard evidence that typically, you would not wear a military uniform when you carried out your duties at Lukavica headquarters, that quite often, you would wear civilian clothes, in particular, a leather jacket. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I usually wear civilian clothes, and I wore a leather jacket because that was the only piece of clothing that I had to put on top of a shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We've heard evidence that it was unusual, in other words, that your civilian dress contrasted to the dress of your fellow officers in the headquarters. Do you agree that other officers in Lukavica headquarters did not wear civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All members of the group for liaising with UNPROFOR, with the exception of Colonel Zarkovic, would wear civilian clothes from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were never requested to wear such uniform except at the meetings -- well, they probably thought that a more -- a closer contact could be established if we wore civilian clothes. I mean, I don't see any particular reason for either wearing civilian clothes or not wearing civilian clothes. Perhaps the reason was because officially, we never -- we didn't carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We've heard evidence that at high-level meetings with the UN, that is, meetings between such persons and General Galic, that you would attend in civilian clothes and it seemed entirely inappropriate. What would you say about that? If I could be more specific, that it Indjicated a considerable degree of power on your part that you didn't have to wear a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see what kind of power can be demonstrated with a particular type of clothes. As far as all meetings with UNPROFOR that were held at the Sarajevo airport, I'm referring to the mixed group meetings, I always attended such meetings in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask the witness be shown a document, it's P3777. It's a document which was on the Defence exhibit list for this witness. And I ask that the B/C/S version be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, when you're handed the document, just look at the first page which is in B/C/S. Don't look at the other pages yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: After the witness has looked at it, perhaps it could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document? In other words, have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the form of the document. However, I have never seen this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you see at the bottom -- I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the witness can place the document on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that General Galic can also see it. Perhaps it could be zoomed in a bit, and especially those parts attention is drawn to that they are zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the form of the document? Does it appear to be an order from General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order signed by the then chief of staff, Colonel Marcetic who signed the order for General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please slowly read in B/C/S the words which appear in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Despite numerous warnings on the 29th of January, 1993, in a greater area of 906 grid reference, an event occurred comparable to the one that had happened in Lapisnice when the Poturice took possession of Mala Kula, thereby creating conditions to endanger the vital communication route Hresa/Radava/Vogosca by taking position of Poljine hill, grid reference 703."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is it addressed to the commander personally of the 1st Romanija Brigade of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is addressed to the commander of the 1st Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does it order the commander on that day and the following day, amongst other things, to carry out an attack to retrieve the Mala Kula in the region of elevation 906 from the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, an attack is being ordered with a purpose of taking back possession of Mala Kula and also taking possession of the previous position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Did that attack succeed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please come back to the first paragraph. You read out the word "Poturice." What is a literal translation of that word into English?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Converts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Converts. And did you understand that to refer to Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, may I remind you the time I granted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I'll only be a another few minutes or few questions if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not very convenient. Because I said not more than ten minutes. And you take a few more minutes, it would leave insufficient time for the Defence to re-examine and the Judges to examine the witness. So one or two questions and not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suggest to you, sir, that is a derogatory term. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, it is a customary term which does carry a certain amount of contempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I have a question for you. In the translation, we have those words, "derogatory term for Muslim converts, and small tower". I suppose those words are not in the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I would suggest to you that 20 minutes for re-examination if any needed should be the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon. In order to save time, whenever possible please respond with yes or no. A moment ago, it was mentioned that there was random indiscriminate targeting. Can you tell us in that respect how accurate a 120 millimetre mortar is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that by profession. I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please wait until I've finished the interpretation. I didn't hear the last words of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More than 50 kilos at any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the last words of the witness because you started speaking already. Would you please refrain from doing so, because it takes more time to redress it. Could you please complete your answer. You've said, at least that's what was translated to us. "I don't know that by profession." Could you please tell us what you then said after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of formation, I'm a communications officer. I was in charge of telecommunications.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But in your opinion, was it possible to fire such a weapon if it is relatively heavy?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. It doesn't arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if -- I think it stems from the cross-examination. Mr. Ierace spent quite some time inquiring about an intervention of an officer. This stems directly from the cross-examination. Let us move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if there was any obligation for the crew to be -- for the UN members to be as close as possible to the artillery pieces that they were required to control?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the agreement concerning the control of the artillery pieces was signed, the UN had the obligation to control such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will change the topic and would like to show the witness the exhibit which was just shown to the witness, 3777. And we will work in the English translation. I should like you to tell us, please in whichever language you prefer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I could imagine, and you might have deduced from the question of Judge Nieto-Navia that the Chamber usually is not pleased by receiving instead of translations, commented translations. So if you are working from the English text, fine. But then I think we cannot ask then the Prosecution any more to provide us a virgin translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, do you wish the B/C/S also?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will work on the B/C/S text, but it doesn't seem quite legible to me. But it will perhaps be better for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, would you please tell us about the part that follows immediately after the word Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In accordance with the established procedure --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: As usual, they did not inform us about this at all and we did not receive their evening report until 21.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, would you agree with me -- strike that. Were there many other cases, to your knowledge, when the information coming from the brigade failed to reach the level of the corps as it seems to follow from this report?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer the question because I do not have any such knowledge. I was not part of the control and command system, that is, of the hierarchy that normally received such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. A moment ago or yesterday, I'm not sure, you Indjicated that 80 per cent of protests were made verbally. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that. I said that about 95 per cent of protests were lodged in verbal form.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for correcting me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my recollection is that was in chief, and there was some problem with the translation. But in essence, my objection is that was in chief, and not in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well the question has been answered now, but the matter has been raised in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, but this was not my question. I first lay the foundation for the question which will follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question is as follows -- yes, thank you. A moment ago the Prosecution asked you if you really do not remember having received specific protests concerning opening fire on civilians, and your answer was "I do not remember." I now want to know the following: In view the fact that 95 per cent of the protests were made verbally, and also in light of the fact that you told us that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps first, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, can finish his question. I've forgotten to put on my microphone. Could Mr. Piletta-Zanin finish his question and you wait --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In light of the percentage of these verbal protests and in light of your testimony that no written record was made thereof, if these protests, whatever they were had arrived, had reached someone else and not yourself, would it have been technically possible that you could have known something about these protests, considering the fact that they were made verbally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's difficult to make this objection in the presence of the witness. I submit that my learned colleague has misstated the evidence of the witness in a critical respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider it. And perhaps in order not to send the witness in and out, could you first move to your next question, and I'll write down that this issue is still pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will gladly move to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you told us about the closing down, or rather the limited use or the interest of the PTT building concerning a kidnapping of a Croat liaison officer. Could you be more specific and providing us with some more details concerning this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I stand to be corrected. I don't recollect anything being said about the kidnapping of a Croat liaison officer. I apologise in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Mr. Ierace withdraws his objection, as far as I understand. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can I have your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim forces captured and detained the official HVO liaison officer upon insistence on the part of the UN, the person was released, and the office in the PTT building that they used was closed down. So only two warring factions had their liaison officers and not all three of them as was initially envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is a question of principle. Do you know as far as the brigade level is concerned, who -- the person responsible for the artillery group within a brigade, from whom is he supposed to receive his orders?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All orders at the level of the brigade are in principle issued by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. If an order to open fire is given to this brigade commander, by whom would it have been?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have received the order from the superior command, that is, the corps command, usually the corps commander, in his absence, the chief of staff. Or in the absence of the chief of staff, the duty operation officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Even in the case of an order to stop firing if any firing is underway?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is the same. I mean, the same structures and the same individuals would have been concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Would there have been any reason for a artillery group commander to receive an order, either to open fire or to stop firing, by a simple liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if such an order would have arrived from a liaison officer, he would not -- he could not carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Ms. Pilipovic has a couple of questions she would like to put to the witness, and then we will conclude our re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to show a document to Mr. Indjic. It's Document Number 1840.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1840. I apologise. Your Honour, I can provide the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be simpler, perhaps. Could it be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Tendered or...?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, in response to a question from Mr. Ierace, you read out certain paragraphs from this document, but could you read out paragraph 2, which starts with "the most characteristic."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most characteristic examples of serious violations of cease-fire are the following: During the whole day, heavy infantry fire directed at the positions in the Okruglica region."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Indjic, is this a type of written protest which has to do with violations of a truce?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Judge Nieto-Navia has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You said during your testimony the following, I'm not going to quote exactly, but you said that the number of UN military observers and the mandate that they had reflected negatively on their possibility to see the situation and to understand it. I would like you to elaborate a little bit on this.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be best to start at the end, perhaps. The mandate of the military observers was very restricted, and it was mostly in force for a period of six months. They came from various regions, these regions included Bangladesh, Kenya, New Zealand, Australia. So it was very difficult for them to become familiar with the real situation on the ground in a course of a six-month period, to become familiar with the units, the people, the men. As far as their number is concerned, it wasn't sufficient for them to be able to cover adequately the wide area of the SRK. They couldn't adequately monitor and report on the overall activities of in that area. And for this reason, several observation posts were established from which direct monitoring -- observation of the activities in the field was not carried out. But the officers simply received a pile of information from various sources on the ground. Very often, the military observers were forced, because of these deficiencies, to forward information that they received from one of the warring factions, and they forwarded this information from one of the warring factions to another warring faction without checking it. I don't know if my answer is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to clarify two matters. And could you please answer my questions as briefly as possible. In the course of your testimony and in response to a question put to you with regard to fire which was opened in Dobrinja in June 1993, and the target was a football match, I'm not sure whether you remember the question that was put to you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the question had to do with the incident in the queue for humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also said, and I'm quoting you in English "All of Sarajevo under Muslim control were civilian areas, and any protest regarding activity in or against Sarajevo was a protest regarding civilians."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for interrupting, but we haven't had any translation into English beyond the point of the quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's page 49, line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the problem is that we didn't receive any translation after your quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quoted the witness who said "all parts of Sarajevo under Muslim control were civilian areas and any protest regarding activity in or against Sarajevo was a protest regarding civilians." And at that point, I said it was at page 49, line 6. And I wanted to be sure of what the witness wanted to say. I wanted to be sure of the meaning of the witness's sentence when he said that the city of Sarajevo was a civilian zone. Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said this, I emphasised how particular the Sarajevo battlefield was because the entire city of Sarajevo is a civilian zone if you observe it from one perspective. If you observe it from another perspective, it is a military zone. That is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So any shelling of the town, in your opinion, amounts to the shelling of a civilian zone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat this again. Because of the specific nature of the Sarajevo battlefield, the entire city of Sarajevo was at the same time a civilian area and a military area. Any action against a military target in Sarajevo was also action taken and directed at a civilian part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it means that a civilian target is also involved. That is the translation of your answer, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that any action directed against a military target in Sarajevo is also action in a civilian area because of the specific nature of the battlefield. The entire area of Sarajevo is at the same time a military area and a civilian area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. And my last question has to do with the letter addressed by the SRK command to General Rose and Soubirou. Do you remember this protest? Madam Registrar, could you help me, please. The document is D1840. Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- this type of document is familiar to me, but I don't remember this document, this specific document from that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you explained that this protest did not satisfy the criteria you had established for an adequate protest, that is to say, it didn't include all the necessary information. Yes, are you confirming that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I am therefore wondering what was the purpose of this protest?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you examine the contents, all contents of this protest, you will see that in general, it has to do with the violation of the truce, the purpose of this protest is by documenting -- by recording the violation of the truce and via the mediation of the UN, the enemy side is supposed to be forced to respect the truce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But this is the point at which I'm no longer following you. You say at the same time that it is a protest, and also that it doesn't satisfy the criteria that you yourself had established in order to consider a protest as a valid protest.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If individual parts of this protest, each part of the protest was separated, and if separate protests were made out of them, then these would be adequate protests and concrete measures could be taken. But this protest is of a general kind, and it does not -- the individual incidents haven't been listed in order for steps to be taken with regard to the individual instance. It's a general protest in order to re-establish the truce that had been violated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got a few questions for you as well, Mr. Indjic. My first question is when protests were made to you, oral protests, did you ever spontaneously comment on these protests? So before seeking information from the ground, did you ever spontaneously respond?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never spontaneously responded to the person who made the protest. But I'm sure that I myself made spontaneous comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Spontaneous comments to who?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] For myself. [Interpretation] For myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They could not be heard by the person who lodged the protest if it was an oral protest?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then may I ask you about uniforms. Was there a standard uniform? Because you testified that military men wearing black caps with human skulls on it were part of the SRK. Where would that cap come from? Was it part of officially prescribed uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those clothes weren't part of the regular uniforms. There was a problem with uniforms from the very beginning of the war so that in various parts, you could see soldiers wearing various kinds of uniforms. The black cap Indjicates a certain ideological position of a given unit and in a conflict with the enemy, attempts were made at all levels to prevent ideological conflicts between -- among the Serbs. And thus, no one requested that these ideological symbols be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question is you said Mr. Ashton had far more authority than just being a photographer. Could you please explain to us what specifically made you believe that he had far more authority?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember this correctly, I think that one of the UNHCR coordinator was Mr. Peter Deck [phoen]. I don't know what basis John Ashton was able to influence many things with regard to the UNHCR activity through this person as a freelance photographer. The doors to the Sarajevo sector command was opened to him. He could go there and contact various people in the command, although he wasn't in the UN chain. And these are some of the factors which led me to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, how did you know all this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through personal information I had and information I obtained from other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions for you. Is there any need to put addition questions to the witness that do arise out of the questions by the Bench? If not -- yes, I was informed that you wanted to address the Chamber for another issue. Please tell us what you would like to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yesterday you asked me to write down the name of the interpreter. I have done so. I didn't want to forget this. And secondly, I wanted to say that I apologise for looking at the Defence accidentally. This wasn't for any particular purpose. I just was not aware of the fact that I should not do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber noticed that on more than one occasion, you did so. The name, Madam Registrar, perhaps you could read out what the witness had written down when dealing with the documents, if it's legible. Well, the name is not very problematic. It's Milanovic, Jadranka. So I think that's easy to catch. I see it's perfectly written on the screen, apart from the diacritic mark, but that's a technical problem. Mr. Indjic, I would like to thank you for answering questions of both parties and the Bench. It took you more than two days in this courtroom. As you have seen, we all tried to accommodate you so that you could travel back and be at home again in time. I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And thank you for having behaved very correctly towards me as a witness. And if you allow me to do so, I would just like to greet my commander at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you just -- I do understand that you know each other, it would be a bit. Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed that Mr. Piletta-Zanin wants to address the Chamber, and I see that Mr. Ierace is on his feet. So who is going first? Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Very briefly. First of all, this is for the French booth, but that's not the reason for which I wanted to intervene. I suggest that they should pay attention to page 25, 60, 65, 70, and 82. And I am assuming that the French booth is sufficiently aware of what it has to find there. Having said that, Mr. President, next week I might not be present, not from the very beginning, but halfway through the week, I might be absent. I might decide not to be present for a very simple reason, but perhaps we could go into private session very briefly. Or I can say this in public, or in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we were informed in the last break that in respect of next week, the Defence will be calling the three witnesses of fact who have not yet been called. That does not really assist us. We need to know the order of the witnesses, and I would be grateful if the Defence could be required to Indjicate that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood that we start with Witness DP2. And then could you give the next two ones, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the next witnesses on the list of the 24th of January are Knezevic Sasa and Krsman Sinisa. I didn't think that the pace could be quite as rapid. I had a list based on the order we had planned, but I told the registry and the Prosecution that I would make a list for the next week after this working day. My colleague will continue with Witness DP2 next week, and then it's -- Knezevic Sasa and Krsman Sinisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. President. Would you also please clarify the obligation of the Defence to inform the Prosecution of any exhibits that they intend to tender through the accused if they exercise their choice to call the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, that certainly is an obligation. If you want to call the accused because as Indjicated before, the Prosecution should have the possibility to prepare for cross-examination. There is another issue, that is, that in your talks with the Victims and Witness Unit, it seems that the arrangement you have made until now is based on the assumption that the expert witnesses will be examined on from Wednesday or Thursday. If you decide that the accused will testify, of course, it would -- an improper way of using the funds of the Tribunal to have the experts to wait for three, four, five extra days. So even if you don't want to tell us now, and I take it that you at least reserve the right to call General Galic, would you please keep in mind that as far as the funds involved is concerned, that it's not acceptable that the expert witnesses stay in The Hague for a long time where we expected them to stay not more than a couple of days before they start their testimony. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the fact that there are two witnesses who are part of the UN family. I don't think it would be useful to mention their names, but we have them in our mind. And their appearance before this Chamber is still in suspense. So this could pose a chronological problem. I have just received a letter from the section concerned. The Defence is trying as much as possible to accelerate this process. But to a large extent, it doesn't have everything under control here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think they are scheduled for a later period of time. As you may have noticed, Ms. Pilipovic and Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber has always said that the accused should be called before we start examining the expert witnesses and has made specifically reference to the possibility that those witnesses for which you very late applied for the assistance of the Chamber to call them and for which witnesses the Chamber did its utmost best, at least the staff supporting the Chamber to, reach them in time, that if they could not be called before the expert witnesses, we might make an exception for them. But it has always been Indjicated that the accused would not be the last witness of fact, but should not be examined once you have started the examination of the expert witnesses. And the other witnesses, that is a matter of whether they can -- whether they can arrive in time in The Hague and these are rather technical reasons and not strictly procedural reasons. And whenever there would be need, and that has been Indjicated as well, to recall the accused, if he has chosen to testify after we have heard the expert testimony, and the same would of course be true for international witnesses that cannot arrive in due time in The Hague, that the Chamber will certainly positively consider such an application. If it's leading to any conclusion, there's a slight difference between the last witness of fact and not testifying before expert witnesses, because the Chamber has always Indjicated that if these international witnesses could not be -- could not arrive in time in The Hague, that perhaps they would be examined during or after the expert witnesses. But that's for technical reasons, and mainly caused by the very late application to -- for assistance in order to get them in The Hague. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. Because there's a distinct possibility that the accused will not be giving evidence next week, I would also be grateful if we could have confirmed the name of the first expert to be called in that scenario so that we can prepare for that witness as well as the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you received this information. I've a final -- yes. I see that the following order is that we start with Cavoski, and then Kunjadic. There is a letter. And it seems to be addressed to you, Mr. Ierace. And it is from the -- let me just check. The 22nd of January. It's dated. So there you find the order of appearance of the expert witnesses. And then I have a last question. In order for the Chamber to decide whether expertise, for example, contradicting the expert report of Ewa Tabeau would be admitted, we'd like to see what it is. Because there are applications for experts to be added to the expert list. We still have to consider what time to allocate for those witnesses, but we would first like to see what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the expert report of Mrs. Svetlana Radovanovic is a demographic report, and it's a response to Ewa Tabeau's report. The translation into English, Your Honour, I think it will be provided today. The translation will be provided to the registry today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was Indjicated already for last week. But at least I'm glad that we'll then receive it today. May I conclude by thanking again the interpreters and the technical staff who did a marvelous job this week, to thank them for again their flexibility. And we'll adjourn until next Monday in this same courtroom in the afternoon, that's a quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
